one_liner: C++ vector with N inline slots (default 8). It skips std::vector's heap allocation while the vector stays small.
what_it_does: fastcpp::small_vector<T, N> keeps its first N elements (default 8) inside the object and moves to a heap buffer only when a push overflows that capacity. It implements part of the std::vector interface: push_back/emplace_back/pop_back, clear, resize(n), reserve, operator[], at, front/back, data, begin/end, size/capacity/empty, plus is_inline() to check that no allocation has happened. It has no insert/erase, assign, swap, shrink_to_fit, comparison operators, reverse iterators, count/range constructors or allocator parameter, so it replaces std::vector only in code that avoids those.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the small-buffer optimization (inline storage). An alignas(T) byte array of N*sizeof(T) is a member, and data_ points into it until the first overflow. Construction, pushes below N and destruction make no allocator calls, and the elements sit in the object's own cache lines, which are usually on the stack. The push_back fast path is one always-inlined size==capacity compare marked unlikely, followed by a placement-new. Growth is in a separate noinline grow() that doubles the capacity. For trivially destructible T, `if constexpr` skips the destructor loop.
when_to_use: Hot loops that create and destroy many short-lived vectors whose size is usually at or below a known small bound (e.g. a few ints or pointers per item), where malloc/free is most of the cost
Function-local temporaries on the stack, where the extra N*sizeof(T) bytes are not kept and the elements share cache lines with the rest of the frame
Trivially copyable element types (ints, pointers, small PODs): destruction does no per-element work and an inline copy or move is a short element loop
Call sites that only append, pop, resize, index and iterate, and never insert or erase in the middle
When you want tests or debug asserts to prove the hot path never allocates, via is_inline()
when_not_to_use: Vectors that often grow past N. After the first overflow it is an ordinary doubling heap vector that still carries the unused inline buffer. No row in results/fastest.json measures the overflow or crossover case
Vectors stored in bulk (array elements, hash-map values, long-lived struct members). From the member layout, small_vector<int, 8> is 56 bytes against std::vector's 24, and an empty one costs the same
Code that moves or swaps vectors a lot. Moving an inline vector moves each element instead of stealing a pointer, and without a swap member std::swap does three O(size) moves
Code that needs the rest of the std::vector API (insert, erase, assign, comparisons, resize(n, value), (n, value) or iterator-range constructors, custom allocators) or exception safety while growing

Teams that need a reviewed, supported dependency. The code is in a private single-author repo. The header has one commit and 4 unit tests (inline-until-overflow, std::string elements, move of inline storage, resize/pop), and the tracker has no issues

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library for this header, which includes only fastcpp/core/bits.hpp and fastcpp/core/macros.hpp. Copy those three files. add_subdirectory plus fastcpp::fastcpp is much heavier, because the INTERFACE target links all ten vendored libraries (fmt, phmap, xsimd, zpp_bits, the two queues, simdjson, yyjson, CRoaring, pocketfft)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 for this header (bits.hpp uses <bit>/std::countl_zero and std::is_constant_evaluated). The repo's CMake requires C++23, and its README lists gcc 13+, clang 17+ or MSVC 19.35+. The benchmark was built with gcc 13.3 at -std=c++20
integration.platforms: any: portable C++ with no intrinsics in this header. CI builds and tests with gcc and clang on Linux and clang on macOS, plus ASan+UBSan on Linux. The macros have MSVC branches, but MSVC is not in CI
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the class has no internal synchronization
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the type is small_vector<T, N> rather than std::vector<T>, and only a subset of the API exists (push_back/emplace_back/pop_back/clear/resize(n)/reserve/[]/at/front/back/data/begin/end/size/capacity/empty). There is no insert, erase, emplace(pos), assign, swap, shrink_to_fit, ==/<, cbegin or rbegin, const at(), count/range constructors or Allocator parameter

gotchas: Pushing an element of the same vector when it is full is unsafe. emplace_back calls grow() before building the new element, and grow() moves the old elements out, destroys them and frees the old heap buffer. So v.push_back(v[0]) at size()==capacity() reads a moved-from or freed object, a case std::vector handles. This comes from reading grow()/emplace_back; no test covers it.

Moving an inline small_vector invalidates pointers, references and iterators to its elements, because they are rebuilt in the destination; a std::vector move keeps element addresses. The moved-from vector is cleared.

grow() gives no exception safety. If an element's copy or move throws partway through, the new buffer leaks and the already-destroyed source elements stay counted in size(), so the destructor destroys them a second time.
Once it spills to the heap it never goes back inline. clear(), resize() and copy-assignment keep the heap buffer and there is no shrink_to_fit; only move-assigning into it frees the buffer.
verified_claims_summary: In the repo's own bench_doing_less, building, summing and destroying 50,000 vectors of 4 ints cost 1.856 ns per vector with small_vector<int, 8> and 39.6 ns with a std::vector<int> that was not reserve()d (libstdc++, 21.3x). The build was gcc 13.3.0 at -O2 -march=native on a shared 4-core Xeon @ 2.10GHz VM, minimum of 7 samples. Under 1->2->4 growth the baseline pays three malloc/free pairs and two reallocations per vector, so the figure is no allocation against un-reserved growth, not one allocation against none. The row (run 2026-09-02-core, commit dfa74f2) was recorded before the repo switched its benchmarks to -O3 and has not been re-measured since.
status_note: The repo is PRIVATE (private:developer-source, 0 stars, readable only with access). It was last pushed 2026-09-04, but this header has had one commit since it was added on 2026-09-02. It is MIT-licensed and small (227 lines plus two helper headers), so copying it into your tree is the practical way to use it.
